description: Reading design choices in a production and explaining the meanings they generate for the audience.
content_html:
Design Is Not Decoration

A common misconception is that set, lighting, sound and costume are the “backdrop” to the real action of the performers. In any well-made production, design is as much a language as speech. A single lighting choice — a green wash sliding in at the moment a character tells their first lie — can communicate to the audience something the dialogue never says. Your job in the exam is to decode that language.

The principle is the same as for performers: name the specific design choice, explain how it was executed technically, and evaluate its effect on the audience. The vocabulary is different — you are now working in lantern types, gobos, underscore, set materials — but the analytical method is identical.

Key Fact

Design vocabulary the examiner rewards: Fresnel (soft-edged wash), profile (hard-edged beam), flood (wide area wash), moving light, gobo (patterned effect), gel (colour filter), lighting special (a single focused lantern on one area), blackout, cross-fade, lighting state.

Lighting: Four Questions to Ask

When you observe a lighting moment in a production, run through four questions:

  1. Direction: where is the light coming from? Front lighting is naturalistic; side lighting gives a dramatic split-face effect and implies conflict or duality; top lighting isolates and can suggest divine or oppressive power; back lighting creates silhouette, suggesting mystery or the loss of individual identity.
  2. Colour: what gel or filter is being used? Cool blues and greens signal isolation, threat or the supernatural; warm ambers and yellows signal domestic warmth, nostalgia or golden-age memory; deep red can signal passion, danger or violence. The specific combination matters — a blue wash with a single warm special on one character separates them from the world around them.
  3. Intensity: what is the brightness? A fade to near-darkness before a final moment creates dread; a sudden full-white wash can feel clinical, exposing, accusatory. The rate of the fade or the snap of the change is also a choice — a snap blackout shocks; a slow two-minute fade mourns.
  4. Equipment and effect: if a gobo projects bars across the stage, does that suggest imprisonment? If a lighting special follows a character across the stage, does that suggest they are watched, celebrated or exposed? Note the effect, not just the equipment.

Imagine you saw a fictional production of a thriller at a hypothetical studio theatre in 2025. In the penultimate scene, the villain revealed their true identity to the protagonist. Consider how a strong analysis might read:

Weak version: “The lighting was dark and dramatic, which suited the tense mood.”

Strong version: “As the villain turned to face the protagonist, the stage lighting cross-faded from a warm amber general wash to a single cold tungsten profile focused tightly on the villain’s face from a steeply raked angle above and stage left. The cross-fade took approximately four seconds, so by the time the speech began the protagonist’s face had vanished into shadow while the villain’s was fully lit — a visual metaphor for the shift in power within the scene. The bar gobo projected across the downstage area suggested confinement; the protagonist was already, in lighting terms, trapped before a word had been spoken. The effect on the audience was palpable: the laughter from earlier scenes disappeared completely, replaced by a sustained, uncomfortable silence.”

Notice: lantern type (profile), direction (steeply raked, stage left), colour (cold tungsten), a gobo type (bar), the rate of the change (four seconds), the metaphorical meaning and a specific audience reaction. All from one lighting cue.

Sound: Diegetic, Non-Diegetic and Soundscape

Diegetic sound is sound the characters can hear; non-diegetic sound is heard only by the audience. A creaking door is diegetic; the unsettling low-frequency drone beneath a scene of domestic abuse is non-diegetic underscore. Both can be analysed for meaning.

When analysing sound, note: the texture of the sound (is it crisp and close, or distant and reverberant?), its placement (coming from specific speakers — stage left, from above, or surrounding the audience?), its relationship to the action (does it start before the scene begins, establishing mood before the performers enter?), and any sudden change (a silence that was filled with underscore is often more powerful than the music itself).

A soundscape is a layered sonic environment rather than a single cue: the simultaneous combination of rain, distant thunder, traffic and an indistinct crowd for an opening city scene, for instance. Note how many layers you can identify and what the cumulative effect was.

Set and Costume: Symbol and Material

Set designers make choices about material, colour, scale, level and symbolic meaning. A single chair on an otherwise bare stage can communicate isolation, power or waiting. A set that rotates during the performance communicates flux, the relentlessness of time, or the character’s inability to escape their world. When analysing set, note: what objects are present and what they symbolise; whether the set changed during the performance and what the change communicated; the relationship between the set’s scale and the performer’s body (a small figure dwarfed by an enormous set reads as the individual overwhelmed by forces beyond their control).

For costume, examiners want specific fabric, colour and silhouette analysis, not just era or genre. A costume that is visually impeccable but slightly too large for the performer communicates something very different from one that fits perfectly. Note colour against the set and against other characters’ costumes — if every character wears grey and one wears deep scarlet, that contrast is a design intention, not an accident.

Students frequently write design analysis at a level of generality that earns little credit: “the lighting was atmospheric,” “the costumes were period-appropriate,” “there was dramatic music.” These sentences do not tell the examiner anything analytical.

Compare “the costumes were period-appropriate” with “the lead character’s costume was a knee-length coat in heavyweight charcoal wool with a silhouette that was structured at the shoulders and narrowed at the waist, giving the performer the physical presence of authority even when standing still.” Both sentences are about costume. Only one demonstrates that you understand how design communicates meaning.

The rule is simple: if you cannot say which lantern, what colour, which fabric and what effect, your note-taking in the theatre was not specific enough. Build the habit of technical precision at the performance itself.

Key Fact

Design disciplines to cover in your review: lighting (lantern type, direction, colour, intensity, gobo, lighting state), sound (diegetic / non-diegetic, texture, placement, underscore, soundscape), set (material, level, scale, symbolic props), costume (colour, fabric, silhouette, fit).
exam_tip_html:
For questions asking you to analyse design choices, the most common error is describing general mood rather than naming specific elements. “The lighting was dark and scary” earns no credit. “A Fresnel flood at 15% intensity with a deep blue gel created a cold, low-contrast environment in which every performer appeared shadowless and exposed” earns marks at every level.

For the 8-mark designer question, you must specify a design discipline (lighting, sound, set or costume) and name concrete elements within it — lantern type, gobo, fabric, colour, fitting. Justify each choice with reference to the moment’s meaning or the directorial intention. Generic descriptors like “dark mood” or “period costume” alone do not demonstrate design knowledge.

In the 32-mark live theatre review, you must address at least one design discipline alongside your performer analysis. The mark scheme rewards responses that show the interaction between performance and design — how a performer’s vocal choice and a lighting state worked together at a specific moment to produce a combined effect on the audience.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Design analysis requires specific technical vocabulary: lantern type, direction, colour, intensity and gobo for lighting; diegetic or non-diegetic, texture, placement and soundscape for sound; fabric, colour, silhouette and fit for costume; material, scale, level and symbolic meaning for set.
  • Run four questions on any lighting moment you observe: What is the direction? What is the colour? What is the intensity? What equipment or effect is being used and what does it mean?
  • General descriptions earn no marks. If you cannot specify which lantern, which colour and which effect at a named moment, return to your production notes and find more detail before you write.

practice_questions.text: Identify one type of lantern used in stage lighting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: Fresnel / profile / flood / moving light / birdie / strobe. Accept any legitimate lantern type from theatrical practice.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'soundscape'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a soundscape is made up of multiple sound layers; 1 mark for explaining that the layers are combined to create an immersive sonic environment that establishes location, period or mood for the audience.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer's use of a gobo can communicate meaning to the audience at a specific moment in a production.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for accurately defining a gobo as a shaped template inside a lantern that projects a pattern of light; 1 mark for naming or describing a specific pattern (e.g. bar gobo suggesting imprisonment, leaf gobo suggesting a natural environment, window-frame gobo placing the action inside a building); 1 mark for explaining the effect on the audience's reading of the scene (e.g. the bars reinforce the theme of confinement visually even as the dialogue speaks of freedom); 1 mark for a developed evaluative statement or link to directorial intention.

practice_questions.text: In the live production you have seen, explain how one lighting choice and one sound choice worked together at a specific moment to create meaning for the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Identifies a specific moment in the production; names a precise lighting choice (lantern type, colour, direction, intensity or effect) and a precise sound choice (type, texture, placement, diegetic or non-diegetic status); analyses how the two choices worked in combination to create a specific audience effect; makes an analytical statement about what the director was trying to communicate through this design combination; language is technically fluent and uses accurate terminology throughout.
Secure (7-9): Both a lighting and a sound choice are named and explained with reasonable specificity; audience effect is identified; some analysis of intention present; mostly accurate terminology.
Developing (4-6): Lighting and sound choices identified but described generally; limited technical vocabulary; some attempt at effect or intention but not developed.
Emerging (1-3): General descriptions only; no technical vocabulary; no analysis of intention or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Imagine you are a lighting designer working on a fictional production of a ghost story at a hypothetical studio theatre. In the scene where the protagonist first sees the ghost, design the lighting state you would use. Refer to specific lighting choices and explain their intended effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Names at least two specific lighting elements (e.g. a cold profile special at steep angle from above stage right for the ghost; a Fresnel wash in a deep blue-green gel across the full stage; a bar gobo projected across the protagonist suggesting entrapment); each choice is justified with reference to its intended audience effect (e.g. the steep top-light creates deep shadows on the ghost's face that deny the audience a clear identity for the figure, creating unease); language is technically fluent.
Secure (5-6): At least two lighting choices named and justified; audience effect explained for at least one; generally specific but may have one general descriptor.
Developing (3-4): Relevant lighting ideas present but described in general terms (e.g. 'I would make the lighting dark and spooky'); limited technical vocabulary; effect mentioned but not developed.
Emerging (1-2): One or two general lighting ideas with no technical vocabulary and no link to audience effect or design intention.

practice_questions.text: Analyse and evaluate the live theatre production you have seen. In your answer, focus on how the design choices (in at least two design disciplines) communicated meaning to the audience. Reach a substantiated evaluative judgement about how successfully the design realised the directorial concept.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (25-32): Detailed, sustained analysis of at least two design disciplines; every design choice is named with technical specificity (lantern type, gobo, gel colour, fabric, soundscape texture); every choice is anchored to a named moment and linked to a stated audience effect; the response evaluates the overall success of the design in realising the directorial concept with substantiated judgement; fluent technical language throughout.
Secure (17-24): At least two design disciplines addressed with reasonable specificity; audience effect identified for most choices; an evaluative judgement present; some technical language.
Developing (9-16): Design choices identified but described generally; limited technical vocabulary; some attempt at audience effect; limited or absent evaluative judgement.
Emerging (1-8): Largely descriptive; one discipline only or very general across both; no technical vocabulary; no evaluative judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: What is a gobo in stage lighting?
options: A type of sound effect used to create ambience
A coloured filter placed over a lantern to change the colour of the light
A shaped template inside a lantern that projects a pattern onto the stage
A lighting state used at the end of a scene

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a diegetic sound?
options: A musical underscore played beneath the dialogue
A telephone ringing that the characters react to
A thunder effect heard only by the audience

knowledge_checks.q: A _____ is a composite of multiple sound layers built up to create an immersive sonic environment.
A _____ lantern produces a soft-edged wash of light, while a _____ produces a hard-edged, focusable beam.
Match each design choice to the technical term that describes it:
left: A specific combination of lanterns active at a given moment
Non-diegetic music played continuously beneath dialogue
A single lantern focused on one small area

flashcard_questions.a: A specific combination of lanterns, colour, direction and intensity active at a given moment.
A shaped template inside a lantern that projects a pattern of light onto the stage.
A single lantern focused on one small area, creating an isolated pool of light.
A lantern producing a soft-edged wash of light, adjustable in beam size.
A lantern producing a hard-edged, focusable beam of light.
Sound that exists within the world of the play and can be heard by the characters.
Sound heard only by the audience, outside the world of the play.
Non-diegetic music or ambient sound played continuously beneath dialogue to support mood.
A composite of multiple sound layers combined to create an immersive sonic environment.

flashcard_questions.q: What four questions should you ask about any lighting moment you observe?
flashcard_questions.a: Direction; colour; intensity; equipment or effect used.

flashcard_questions.q: What specific details should you note about a costume to earn marks in analysis?
flashcard_questions.a: Colour, fabric, silhouette, fit, and any accessories or symbolic elements.

flashcard_questions.q: What does top lighting typically communicate to an audience?
flashcard_questions.a: Isolation, divine power, or an oppressive external force bearing down on the character.
A broad, even spread of light covering a large area of the stage, establishing general atmosphere.

glossary_terms.definition: A shaped template placed inside a lantern to project a pattern of light onto the stage, such as window bars, leaves or abstract shapes.
A specific combination of lanterns active at a given moment, defined by direction, colour, intensity and type.
A single lantern focused on one small area of the stage, creating an isolated pool of light around one performer or object.
A layer of non-diegetic music or ambient sound played continuously beneath the dialogue to support mood and atmosphere.
Sound that exists within the world of the play and can be heard by the characters, such as a ringing telephone or birdsong.
Sound that exists outside the world of the play and is heard only by the audience, such as a musical underscore.
A composite of multiple sound layers built up to create an immersive sonic environment for the audience.
A broad, even spread of light from a flood or Fresnel lantern covering a large area of the stage to establish general atmosphere.
